title: Alternative reinforcers differentially modify cocaine self-administration by humans

claims.statement: In six people who smoked cocaine almost daily, living on an inpatient research unit, cocaine was chosen over a $5 voucher on most occasions but not all: the voucher was taken more often when the cocaine dose was smaller, and slightly more often when it was for cash than when it was for goods, a difference that cannot be separated from the order of the sessions; with no session offering cocaine without an alternative, the study cannot show how much the vouchers lowered cocaine taking. The four women and two men (aged 30 to 39, recruited in New York City by word of mouth and newspaper advertisements, spending $100 to $500 a week on cocaine; whether they wanted treatment is not stated) each completed eight sessions; in each, after a sample trial, they chose five times, 14 minutes apart, between one dose of smoked cocaine (study conditions: 0, a dummy dose, or 12, 25 or 50 mg, one dose level per session) and a $5 voucher, each choice requiring 200 key presses, and the four money-voucher sessions always came before the four merchandise-voucher sessions. Cocaine choices rose with dose (F(3, 15) = 15.26, P < 0.001) and were fewer with the money voucher (F(1, 5) = 7.48, P < 0.05), with no significant difference at any single dose. On the editors' reading of the figures, cocaine was chosen on average 10.7 of 20 times with the money voucher and 12.8 with the merchandise voucher (difference 2.2 choices, 95% CI 0.1 to 4.2, editors' calculation), more than a third of the difference coming from the dummy-dose sessions; with active doses, cocaine was chosen on 60 and 68 of 90 occasions (about 2 in 3 and 3 in 4), at 12 mg about half the time (2.5 and 2.7 of 5) and at 50 mg about 4 times in 5 (3.8 and 4.5 of 5) (Hart et al., 2000). The study measured choices in a laboratory, with small, immediate rewards, not cocaine use outside it; all participants reported using much more cocaine outside the laboratory than in the sessions; the authors' extension to treatment that rewards drug-free tests with vouchers (contingency management) was not tested here; and the earlier laboratory studies they cite, in which larger money alternatives lowered cocaine choice, were not read. Rat studies of choices between cocaine and other rewards are in the answer on the Rat Park studies. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Dose F(3, 15) = 15.26, P < 0.001; kind of voucher F(1, 5) = 7.48, P < 0.05; no significant voucher difference at any single dose. Editors' reading of Figure 2 (totals of 20, money vs merchandise): 15 vs 16, 7 vs 7, 12 vs 14, 12 vs 16, 2 vs 7, 16 vs 17; means 10.7 vs 12.8; mean paired difference 2.17 (95% CI 0.13 to 4.20; dz 1.12; editors' calculation, reproducing the printed F). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (mean choices of 5, money vs merchandise): 0 mg 0.67 vs 1.50; 12 mg 2.50 vs 2.67; 25 mg 3.67 vs 4.17; 50 mg 3.83 vs 4.50; active doses 60 vs 68 of 90 choices; 0.83 of the 2.17 difference (38%) from the dummy-dose sessions.
